extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and novelists interested in using epistolary (letters/journals/texts) format
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting stories told through letters, journal entries, texts, emails, social media posts, and other document formats, including when and how to mix epistolary elements with traditional prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: What epistolary POV is
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey a narrative story through the use of letters, journal entries, or other documents (including emails, text messages, social media posts, police reports, interviews, logs, maps, schematics, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be single-POV (one character's journal/blog) or multi-POV (different documents from different characters). It can function as the whole work or part of a larger traditional-prose narrative. The format you choose should serve how information is revealed and how the story threads together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the right voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the language, tone, and conventions of the chosen document type and time period (e.g., a formal 1890 letter vs. a casual 2022 text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical formats ensure period-accurate diction and references. Include visual cues where appropriate (date, return address, sign-off, signature). For modern communications, reflect real-world brevity and punctuation (rarely full sentences in texts). Use these differences to convey distinct voices and character traits (e.g., a character who replies with GIFs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the voices separate
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure each character's written voice is distinct so voices do not run together in the absence of internal narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about style and tone for each character’s letters/posts. Because epistolary format limits access to internal thoughts, differentiate characters via diction, rhythm, punctuation, medium-specific habits (e.g., emoji use, formal salutations), and consistent quirks. If voices blur, readers may struggle to follow who is 'speaking.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about connections (narrative thread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the collection of disparate documents has a thread that ties them together and reveals the story coherently without over-explaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the temptation to explain everything; instead map out how documents will interrelate to tell the story. Use story mapping and beta-reader feedback to confirm readers can follow the through-line. Balance providing enough information for the story to be understood without beating readers over the head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell (avoid epistolary oversharing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist having letters/journals that recount every detail or full dialogue; prioritize immersive, noticeable details over exhaustive description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realistic personal documents omit many details—focus on what a writer in that situation would actually notice and report (e.g., 'the night was cold and drizzly' vs. listing stars and tactile ground-feel). For full, dynamic scenes (like extended dialogue or action), choose formats better suited to convey them (interview transcripts, phone call logs, text conversation threads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epistolary format strategically for background and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use documents to present background information in an engaging way and to switch between tenses/time periods more easily than block prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistolary pieces can naturally present multiple timelines and allow effortless tense shifts; leverage this for stories with complex chronology or lots of backstory rather than dumping exposition into straight narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose document types and formats that fit content
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the kinds of documents (letters, police reports, court documents, text messages, emails, social posts, logs, blueprints, images) that most plausibly convey the information you need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick formats that justify the information they reveal (e.g., police reports for evidence, texts for quick back-and-forth). For conveying complete conversations, use transcripts or threaded texts; for visual material incorporate images/diagrams when helpful. Mixing varied document types can enrich texture (redactions, flyers, schematics), but ensure each item earns its place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate epistolary elements with traditional prose when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not have to write an entire novel epistolary—mixing in texts or letters within mostly traditional narration can be effective and realistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern novels frequently include occasional text messages or social posts; use them to convey information or show character development without committing the whole work to epistolary form. Ensure transitions between prose and documents feel natural and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor realistic contemporary communication habits
rubrics_metrics.description: For modern settings, portray technology use (cell phones, social platforms, emojis, GIFs, group chats) realistically rather than imposing formal prose conventions onto informal media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People rarely text in full sentences with perfect punctuation—use that realism to characterize and convey tone. Small elements like a character’s habit of replying with GIFs, frequent emoji use, or terse one-word texts can powerfully convey personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by reading examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Study existing epistolary works (classic and modern) to see how authors use different devices and solve structural challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists many examples (e.g., Persuasion, Dracula, Illuminae, The Martian, Bridget Jones's Diary). Reading widely in the subgenre helps you understand possibilities for structure, voice, and inventive use of document types.
